summary: Children aged 9–10 learn to construct a claim–evidence–reasoning argument that links a specific plant or animal structure (internal or external) to how it supports survival, growth, behaviour, or reproduction. The core skill is scientific argumentation (justifying the structure→function→survival-benefit link), not naming structures. Activities exercise building arguments from real observation, critiquing weak arguments, and defending claims under questioning, with explicit attention to internal structures and non-defence functions.
misconceptions: Thinking 'structure' means only external, visible parts, missing internal organs as structures with survival functions.
Stating a survival benefit without linking it to the structure's actual function (asserting rather than reasoning).
Assuming every structure is for defence/predator-avoidance, overlooking growth, behaviour and reproduction functions.
Believing organisms 'chose' or 'grew' structures because they needed them (intentional/Lamarckian framing) rather than structures being features that aid survival.
Confusing a good-sounding statement with a good argument — not noticing when evidence and claim don't actually connect.

activities.title: Build a survival argument workbench
steps: Choose an organism (for example a cactus, a polar bear, or an owl) and observe its structures from a real specimen, photo, or labelled diagram.

Pick one structure (for example cactus spines, thick fur, or sharp talons) and assemble a three-part argument: a CLAIM ('the cactus's spines help it survive'), EVIDENCE ('spines are sharp, narrow, and cover the stem'), and REASONING ('they stop animals eating the cactus and their small surface area reduces water loss, so the cactus survives the hot, dry desert').
Test whether each slot genuinely connects: does the evidence describe the structure, and does the reasoning explain how that function gives a survival benefit?
Spot and reject tempting broken chains that pair the right structure with the wrong benefit, then rebuild a chain that actually links the structure to a survival advantage.
Repeat with at least one INTERNAL structure (for example heart → pumps blood to deliver oxygen and food → keeps the animal alive) so structure is not equated only with visible external parts.
activities.insight: A good argument is not just a true-sounding statement: the evidence must describe the actual structure and the reasoning must explain how its function produces a survival (or growth/behaviour/reproduction) benefit. Rejecting a plausible but disconnected chain and rebuilding a connected one is where the argumentation skill is felt.

activities.title: Question-and-answer with a field biologist
steps: Present a structure-function claim about an organism to a partner, teacher, or in-role 'field biologist' character.
Respond to probing follow-ups: 'And how does that help it survive?', 'What's your evidence?', 'Would broad flat leaves be better or worse in the desert — argue your case.'
Defend or revise the argument when offered a counter-example (for example: 'What if we moved the cactus to a wet rainforest — would its structures still be an advantage? Why?').
Extend the reasoning to an internal structure of an animal, linking it to survival in the same step-by-step way.
activities.insight: Argumentation is dialogic: being pressed for evidence and mechanism, and handling counter-examples, strengthens reasoning and exposes assertions that don't actually connect.

activities.title: Observe real structures and reveal their functions
steps: Examine real or pictured organisms (plant and animal) and locate specific structures: thorns, claws, waxy leaves, roots, heart, lungs.
For each, record what the structure is/does and the survival role it serves, sorting structures into internal versus external.

Check and correct common misconceptions (for example, that spines make food the way leaves do, or that cacti generally store their water in their roots, when most cacti store water mainly in the stem).
activities.insight: Building accurate structure→function knowledge, grounded in observation, gives learners the evidence base their arguments will rest on, and shows that internal organs are structures with survival functions too.

activities.title: Measure surface area and water loss
steps: Set up two identical paper 'leaves' (same paper, same size, same amount of water) — one spread flat (large exposed surface) and one rolled tight like a spine (small exposed surface) — and place them side by side in the same spot; OR coat both surfaces of one real leaf in petroleum jelly and leave a similar-sized leaf from the same plant bare, keeping both in the same conditions.
Before observing, predict which loses water faster and explain WHY.
Weigh or inspect them over a day and compare the result to the prediction.
Use the result as evidence in an argument about why a cactus has narrow spines and a waxy stem rather than broad leaves.
activities.insight: When other conditions are matched, less exposed surface area usually means less water lost, and a waxy coating reduces loss — the same form-function link that helps explain cactus spines and a waxy stem. Results should be read from the actual measurement. Predicting that the flat or uncoated one will dry faster because more of its wet surface is open to the air shows the link has formed; predicting no difference shows it has not yet.

activities.title: Judge strong versus broken arguments
steps: Read pairs of arguments about the same structure — one that connects structure, function, and survival benefit, and one that is weak (right structure, wrong benefit, or a benefit asserted with no mechanism).
Decide which is the stronger argument and say exactly what is missing or broken in the weaker one.
Repair the weak argument by supplying the missing evidence or mechanism.
activities.insight: A good-sounding statement is not automatically a good argument; recognising where evidence and claim fail to connect clarifies what makes reasoning hold.

checkQuestion: A cactus has sharp spines instead of broad leaves, a thick waxy stem, and long shallow roots. Pick one of these structures and build an argument: how does it help the cactus survive in a hot, dry desert?
checkAnswer: A reasoned link, for example: spines (modified leaves) have tiny surface area so little water is lost, and they protect the cactus from thirsty animals; OR the thick waxy stem stores water while its waxy coat cuts water loss; OR long shallow roots spread wide to grab rain quickly before it evaporates. The structure's form is tied to the survival function.
